![Post hero image](https://static.wixstatic.com/media/11062b_d9d6aa519ddd49119dc43c77400960f2~mv2.jpg/v1/fill/w_1000,h_563,al_c,q_85,usm_0.66_1.00_0.01/11062b_d9d6aa519ddd49119dc43c77400960f2~mv2.jpg)

In this post, I use model weights plus a fixed SAE feature basis trained
beforehand, to map what kinds of routing and writing patterns are
available inside attention heads (i.e., what the head’s linear maps make
possible in this fixed SAE coordinate system, not what it necessarily
uses on typical tokens) without collecting new activations or running
generation. This allows us to study what a given attention head linearly
implements in this feature basis.

I’ll show the core measurement objects, then use them to build a
depth-wise “map” of head behavior in Gemma-2: how sliding vs global
attention layers seem to differ, how routing sharpness and
identity-sensitivity evolve with depth, and how write behavior shifts
from early to late layers.

What this post is: a “map-making” update. Readable, falsifiable.

What this post is not: a claim that any specific head is “the” cause of
a specific behavior.

Weight-space gives us leverage + structure; sign and task relevance
still require experiments which I will follow up in Post 2 and beyond.

## SETUP

We use the base model Gemma-2-2B (26 layers).

It uses GQA: 8 query heads and 4 KV heads, so each KV head is shared by
2 query heads.

1.  Gemma‑2 scales attention logits by
    \({query\_pre\_attn\_scalar}^{-1/2}\). With query_pre_attn_scalar =
    256, we have \(s = \sqrt{\frac{1}{256}} = \frac{1}{16} = 0.0625\).

2.  Softcap value: \(c = 50.0 \).

3.  Gemma-2 uses sliding window attention in alternating layers starting
    at index 0: even layers are sliding-window with size 4096, odd
    layers are global (full causal attention up to the model’s max
    context length, 8192 tokens).

To talk about “features” rather than neurons, I use Google's Gemma Scope
Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs). These SAEs are trained on the base models of
Gemma-2 series.

Analysis choice: I use the SAEs trained at the "Residual SAE" tap point
from below diagram. Attention in block L consumes the residual stream
produced by block L−1. Thus, in my runs I use an SAE layer offset (−1)
so the SAE basis matches what the attention block actually sees. Each
SAE feature has a decoder direction (a vector in residual space). I’ll
treat those decoder directions as a convenient, model-aligned basis for
analysis. Please note that SAE decoder directions are not orthogonal and
activations are nonnegative.

Throughout, I fold the learned RMSNorm scale into weights but ignore the
token-dependent normalization factor; this makes the analysis strictly
linear-in-direction rather than exact-in-activation.

Using the base model helps to keep our focus on the attention mechanism
and prevent any artifacts possibly observed as a result of instruction
fine tuning.

*Fig 1: Available Gemma Scope SAEs*

## WEIGHT-SPACE OBJECT #1: CONTENT-ONLY ROUTING IN FEATURE SPACE

For a single attention head, I want a matrix that answers:

“If the query looks like feature i, which key-feature j does this head
prefer?”

Let:

- \(D\) be the SAE decoder matrix for a subset of features (shape n ×
  d_model), one row per feature direction (Convention: I treat decoder
  directions as row vectors; if you store decoders as columns, transpose
  accordingly.)

- $W_{Q}$, $W_{K}$ be the head’s query/key projection matrices

Project decoder directions into Q-space and K-space:

$Q_f = D \cdot W_Q^T$

$K_f = D \cdot W_K^T$

Define the content-only affinity matrix (what attention logits would
look like if RoPE and masking weren’t present):

$B = (Q_f \cdot K_f^T) \cdot s$

Where \(s = \sqrt{\frac{1}{256}} = \frac{1}{16} = 0.0625\) (Gemma‑2’s
attention logit scaling).

Gemma-2 also applies a tanh soft-cap to attention logits; when matching
the model’s behavior, I apply the same cap:

$\text{softcap}(x) = c \cdot \tanh\left(\frac{x}{c}\right)$

This \(B\) matrix is the backbone of our routing analysis. From \(B\) we
can define simple, interpretable routing metrics:

- Selectivity (peakiness): per row i, softmax over keys and take max
  probability; average over i → “top-1 softmax mass”

- Identity sensitivity: how much softmax probability lands on the
  diagonal entry (i attends to i) → “diagonal softmax mass”

- Max-gap: difference between best key score and runner-up (in logits),
  averaged over rows

- Avoidance: Negative entries in \(B\) indicate low dot-product
  affinity. I treat extreme negative tails as a signature of selective
  exclusion, but it’s not the same thing as suppression unless the
  \(OV\) path also writes negative feature directions.

Important: rows/cols of \(B\) are SAE features, not tokens. When I
compute "top‑1 softmax mass", the softmax is over key features j, not
over token positions..

Sanity check: does B predict real attention routing?

Although the map in this post is computed purely from weights plus a
fixed SAE basis, I ran a activation-grounding sanity check to confirm
that the main routing object (the feature affinity matrix B) predicts
runtime attention patterns.

Across 200 heads (25 layers x 8 heads), using all 16,384 SAE features
and RoPE-aware affinity matrices B_delta, the activation-grounding run
covers about 4.45M token pairs per head. Mean overall Spearman rho is
0.07 (std 0.21), while mean local (0-4 token) rho rises to 0.15; 144/200
heads exceed |local rho| > 0.1, and the best local head is L5H4 at rho =
0.82. The layerwise spread and threshold counts are shown in Fig 2(d)
and Fig 2(e).

*Fig 2(d):*

*Fig 2(e):*

For ~25 diverse prompts, I captured the pre-attention residual stream at
the target layer, encoded it into the same SAE feature subset used in
the weight-space map, and predicted attention preferences using the
bilinear form a(t)ᵀ B a(s). For the runtime target, I used log attention
weights. I compute correlations per query row and then average (to avoid
cross-row normalization artifacts), and I also break correlations out by
distance bins; log-softmax equals logits up to a per-row constant, so
rank correlation is meaningful even though each row has its own
normalization.

To account for RoPE, I also computed RoPE-aware affinity matrices BΔ per
distance bin by rotating K (Δ set to the bin center) and applying
Gemma’s tanh softcap, then compared predicted vs runtime attention
within each distance bin.

Results across 200 heads (25 layers × 8 heads), using all 16,384 SAE
features (full dictionary) and RoPE-aware affinity matrices B_Δ per
distance bin:

- ~4.5M token pairs per head

- Mean overall Spearman ρ = 0.07 (std=0.21)

- Mean local (0–4 tokens) Spearman ρ = 0.15 (max=0.82)

- 144 heads (72%) show |local ρ| > 0.1 ('structured' routing)

- Best local correlation: L5H4 with ρ = 0.82

- Best overall correlation: L6H4 with ρ = 0.57

An important caveat: the correlation is not uniform across depth. In
early layers (L1–L5), 35 of 40 heads show positive overall Spearman ρ
(mean +0.16), and mid layers (L6–L12) are even stronger (47/56 positive,
mean +0.22). But in late layers (L19–L25), 50 of 56 heads show negative
overall Spearman (mean −0.14), meaning the weight-space B matrix
predicts the opposite of the observed attention pattern. This
degradation likely reflects nonlinear interactions (LayerNorm, residual
stream composition, or superposition effects) that are not captured by
the linear SAE decomposition. The weight-space map remains a faithful
guide in early/mid layers but should be interpreted with caution past
~Layer 17.

The distribution is heavy-tailed: many heads are near-zero (diffuse),
while a smaller set shows strong, structured routing (e.g., best local ρ
≈ 0.82). The top 10 heads by overall Spearman (L6H4, L5H4, L3H2, L6H3,
L8H1, L8H0, L6H2, L8H6, L12H3, L12H2; all ρ > 0.45) cluster in layers
3–12.

Please note that this doesn’t prove any head is causally responsible for
a behavior; it just checks that the measurement objects used in the map
are anchored to runtime attention.

BASELINES: WHAT COUNTS AS “REAL STRUCTURE”?

Softmax selectivity is extremely sensitive to logit scale, so we need
baselines that match the right thing. I use three baselines, each
designed to kill a different kind of structure:

1.  Random decoder directions (random D): Replace decoder directions
    with random unit vectors (matched norms), keeping W_Q/W_K fixed

2.  Random weights baseline: Replace W_Q and W_K with random matrices
    (same shape), then rescale B to match std(B) before computing
    softmax-derived metrics. Specifically, we rescale B_baseline ←
    B_baseline × (σ_real / σ_baseline), where σ = std(B).

3.  Permuted-K baseline: Shuffle key-feature identities by permuting
    rows of K_f (equivalently, permuting columns of B), so diagonal mass
    becomes ‘chance self-match’.

This lets me say things like:

“Selectivity is X times the random-weights baseline.”

“Diagonal mass is X times the permuted-K baseline.”

Why both matter:

- top-1 mass is permutation-invariant (it only cares that you pick
  something)

- diagonal mass is identity-sensitive (it cares that you pick self)

## WEIGHT-SPACE OBJECT #2: WHAT A HEAD WRITES (OV) IN FEATURE SPACE

Routing is only half the story. Even if a head can attend cleanly, it
only matters if its output projection writes a direction that’s salient
in the SAE feature basis into the residual stream.

For a query head, its write is determined by:

- W_V for the KV group (shared across 2 query heads in Gemma-2 GQA
  implementation)

- W_O for the specific query head

Gemma’s effective OV matrix is implemented as:

W_(OV) = W_(O) W_(V)

For each SAE feature direction dⱼ (row of D), define the write vector:

writeⱼ = dⱼ · W_Vᵀ · W_Oᵀ

Project write vectors back onto decoder directions to get a
“write-to-feature” matrix:

W2F[j,k] = cos(writeⱼ, d_k)

Note: W2F uses cosine similarity, so it measures directional
alignment and discards magnitude; later I’ll also report write norms /
activation-grounded deltas so ‘aligned-but-tiny’ writes don’t get
over-interpreted.

This helps us define archetypes with concrete scoring.

With W2F as the cosine similarity matrix between each feature's write
vector and all decoder directions, we define:

- COPY score = mean(diag(W2F)): how much feature i writes back to itself

- TRANSFORM score = max off-diagonal of W2F: strength of the strongest i
  → j≠i mapping

- BROADCAST score = max column sum of W2F: how many features write to
  the same target

- SUPPRESS score = |min off-diagonal of W2F|: strength of the most
  negative write

Across all 200 heads, mean copy dominance is 0.19 (most heads are
transformative rather than identity-preserving). The strongest copy head
is L2H2 (copy dominance = 0.90), followed by L24H3 (0.90) and L17H7
(0.86). Late-layer copy heads cluster in L23–L25, consistent with the
model needing to preserve and propagate features near the output.

A head is classified by whichever score crosses its threshold first
(COPY > 0.3, TRANSFORM > 0.5, BROADCAST > 3× copy, SUPPRESS > 0.5),
defaulting to DIFFUSE. I assign a single label using a precedence rule
(COPY → TRANSFORM → BROADCAST → SUPPRESS → DIFFUSE). Heads can score
highly on multiple axes; the label is just meant to be a coarse summary.

In this taxonomy, SUPPRESS means the head routes positively to some key
feature j, and then the OV write is negatively aligned with a target
feature k (it is not about negative B/avoidance). Also, please note that
COPY can be negative if the head writes anti-aligned to the feature’s
decoder direction.

WEIGHT-SPACE OBJECT #3: COMPOSING “FEATURE PROGRAMS” (i → j → k)

Once we have routing (B) and writing (W2F), we can compose them into
simple “programs”:

query feature i → attend key feature j → write feature k

Programs are extracted from the top tail of routing scores and write
scores (quantile thresholds), so the taxonomy describes high-confidence
motifs rather than all mass. We also track when a self-write is a
fallback rather than a measured OV target.

Each triplet is scored by combining route strength and write strength.
Then we can classify it into a small motif family:

Table 1: Program Types

```text
+------------+---------------------------+
```
| Type       | Flow                      |
```text
+------------+---------------------------+
```
| REINFORCE  | i → i → i                 |
```text
+------------+---------------------------+
```
| SHIFT      | i → i → k (k≠i)           |
```text
+------------+---------------------------+
```
| CROSS_COPY | i → j → j (i≠j)           |
```text
+------------+---------------------------+
```
| RELAY      | i → j → i (i≠j)           |
```text
+------------+---------------------------+
```
| TRANSFORM  | i → j → k (all different) |
```text
+------------+---------------------------+
```
| SUPPRESS   | i → j → −k                |
```text
+------------+---------------------------+
```

This is the point where the analysis becomes human-legible: you can say
“this head implements a lot of CROSS_COPY” or “this layer is
SUPPRESS-heavy,” without running a prompt.

In my run: routing tail ≈ top 10%; write tail ≈ top 20%.

POSITION ROBUSTNESS: RoPE STABILITY AS A “SEMANTIC CONTROLLABILITY” PROXY

Gemma-2 uses RoPE, which rotates Q/K vectors as a function of relative
position. In weight space you can simulate this by rotating keys (or
queries) and recomputing affinity matrices.

Let B₀ be affinity at relative offset Δ=0, and B_Δ at offset Δ. Define a
stability score (e.g., cosine similarity of flattened matrices):

stability(Δ) = cos(vec(B₀), vec(B_Δ))

Then compress the curve across Δ into a single number (AUC-style over
log-distance). I call this RoPE stability: a summary of how similar the
affinity matrix B stays as we apply relative-position rotations. Also,
we apply the tanh softcap before comparing matrices.

- When this metric is High → routing seems to be mostly
  content-controlled and stays similar across positions. It could also
  mean that this head doesn't use positional information much because
  it's doing something else entirely.

- And when it is Low → routing depends strongly on relative position
  (more “twitchy”).

This is not “style steerability,” but it is a useful proxy for
“position-invariant content routing.”

One caveat: cosine similarity can look high if B is very low-magnitude /
diffuse; I interpret stability alongside routing strength/selectivity.

*Fig 4(a): L24H5 and L17H4 show higher RoPE stability than L25H1 and*
L5H0]

RESULTS: WHAT CHANGES WITH DEPTH?

Once we compute these objects across layers and heads, we can summarize
how the model’s attention machinery evolves with depth.

1.  Local (sliding-window) vs global layers

    Gemma-2 alternates local and global attention by layer, giving a
    built-in contrast:

Sliding-window layers can’t directly attend to tokens outside the
window, but they can still transform a residual stream that already
contains long-range information injected by earlier global layers.

Global layers are the only layers that can implement direct long-range
attention pointers.

*Fig 5(a): Sliding window attention layers show more selectivity*

*Fig 5(b): Sliding window attention layers show more diagonal*
(self-probability) mass]

*Fig 5(b): Sliding window attention layers show more diagonal*
(self-probability) mass

2.  Selectivity and identity-sensitivity are not monotone

    Two different things can happen as depth grows:

1.  Peakiness (top-1 softmax mass) can increase because the model learns
    sharper “addressing”

2.  Identity sensitivity (diagonal softmax mass) can increase if heads
    learn an i→i “feature self-match” pattern

In my current run, there’s a very strong spike in these metrics around a
mid layer (one layer stands out dramatically on both selectivity and
diagonal mass). That suggests a “band” of unusually crisp routing
behavior rather than a smooth trend.

*Fig 6: Sel×U and DiagM×U vs layer*

3.  RoPE stability tends to rise with depth (with bands)

    RoPE stability tends to increase with depth, but it’s not smooth.
    There are high-controllability bands (mid layers and a late cluster
    near the top of the network).

*Fig 7: RoPE stability vs layer*

4.  Writes become more targeted late in the network

    In this run, transform-like write structure is not monotone with
    depth; it concentrates in specific bands. I’ll show that
    distribution rather than claiming a smooth trend.

My intuition: late layers are closer to logits, so targeted writes are
more valuable and weight-space seems to reflect that.

*Fig 8: fraction of TRANSFORM vs BROADCAST heads*

5.  Redundancy vs uniqueness (where structure concentrates)

    I track how redundant heads are within a layer (do they “do the same
    thing” in program space?). Redundancy = Jaccard similarity of top-20
    routing pairs between heads. Two heads are considered redundant if
    they route the same (query_feature → key_feature) pairs highly:

Low redundancy: a few specialized heads carry most structure → could be
potential larger single-head “levers”

High redundancy: many heads share similar top programs → could mean that
the layer is robust to removing any one head

To avoid noise, I primarily interpret redundancy within the subset of
heads that show structured routing (e.g., above a small selectivity or
correlation threshold).

*Fig 9: Within layer attention head features redundancy vs layer*

## WHAT I THINK THIS MEANS

Weight-space analysis is not telling you “what the model will output.”
It’s telling you what kinds of operations are available in the weights,
and where in depth those operations concentrate.

Safest takeaways from this weight-space + SAE-basis analysis:

- Local vs global layers are qualitatively different substrates. If a
  behavior requires long-range access, only global layers can implement
  it directly.

- There are depth bands with unusually crisp routing (spikes in
  selectivity and sometimes identity-sensitive diagonal mass).

- Writes become more transform-like late. Late layers are more likely to
  contain heads whose OV paths implement systematic feature-to-feature
  rewriting.

- Redundancy varies a lot. Some layers look like “few special heads,”
  others spread structure across many heads.

## PREDICTIONS FOR POST 2 (EXPERIMENTS DRIVEN BY WEIGHT-SPACE)

In Post 2, I will test behavior, but driven by pre-registered
weight-space predictions.

One candidate hypothesis: heads with high selectivity and strong
directional write structure (high COPY/TRANSFORM/etc scores) but low
RoPE stability could contribute disproportionately to long-distance
errors on retrieval-style tasks; ablating their OV contribution may
measurably change accuracy (possibly improve or worsen), especially at
large distances.

Update (Jan 2026): I ran causal ablation experiments on Layer 23 — which
the weight-space map flagged as a high-selectivity, high-controllability
layer — ablating individual heads and multi-head combinations (H0,
H1+H6, H4+H5) on retrieval-style prompts with symmetry controls (swapped
A↔B). I also ran a full OV writing validation across all 200 heads
confirming that predicted feature writes match actual head output with
mean cosine similarity of +0.50 in early/mid layers, but flip sign in
late layers (e.g., L20H7 cosine = −0.64), a finding that persists with
the full 16K feature set. Post 2 is forthcoming with full results.

Thank you very much for reading.

Feedback, comments, and discussion are always welcome!

done.

placement, and alternating sliding-window convention are codified in the
project config.

## APPENDIX: METRIC GLOSSARY

- top1_mass = mean over query features of max softmax probability across
  keys

- Sel×U = top1_mass ÷ (1/n)

- diagonal_softmax_mass = mean softmax mass on the diagonal entry
  (identity-sensitive)

- DiagM×U = diagonal_softmax_mass ÷ (1/n)

- max_gap = average(top1_logit − top2_logit) per row

- semantic_controllability = summary of how stable B remains under
  RoPE-relative rotations

- COPY / TRANSFORM / BROADCAST / SUPPRESS = write archetypes derived
  from W2F

- Feature programs = composed triplets i → j → k with a small taxonomy
